chapter: Defending the music and its origins
title: Faking, funerals, parade bands, and ragtime versus jazz rhythm
summary: La Rocca describes how fakers invented jazz licks, says Negro bands did not play carnival parades or funerals in his day, and distinguishes ragtime's jumping rhythm from jazz's smooth rhythm.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: would have to make up such stuff to fake, like brrrr through a horn. And different other little things that he didn't know the tune would add, different little things, which later became known as jazz licks or jazz idioms. It was just like a fake, a bunch of gypsies, didn't know nothing. And not knowing the tune, we'd fall back on it. Now I could tell you, many of the fellows, they put them all together these tunes, these idioms. They'll start do all together. When he finished that one chord construction with that tune, let me see him play another tune behind it. Well I didn't do that. I could have played the same way. But after I finish one tune in that same chord construction, they were all alike, they became all alike. There was no difference. So I was a limited man. I limited my licks. I limited the different little things that I could put into it, saving it for somewhere else for a little novelty. So he played straight. That's true. I stuck to the melodic line. You know what I was playing. Well, did you know what the Negro followed me with playing? It says he built it on chords. That's a lie. He built it on my tunes in the marches that I played around the streets that they played in the carnival parades. Because no Negro played the carnival parades. They may have played in marching bands, and I don't remember them in my early times playing in marching bands. And as far as the funerals, they never played them in my days. That's all only lately since the jazz club to give credence that these people buried them by... This marching business, a march, a burial, came in with the military first. Then come the societies. Then come the different other people like the volunteer fire department, which I played. I played four different funerals for them. Jacqueline had the job, but I was the leader of the job. And they'd have a few men that read. I was a faker. But once I heard a tune, I could play it. And if I didn't play it, what I played never went against what the other man was playing. Because it would be either a harmony note or another note that would coincide with what he was playing. And many of the tunes, like Flea is a Bird, this fellow Papi, that this is one of the men that had bands out on the road too. He would be the cornet player. And he played a melody, and I'd play along with him. He had rock on baritone. He was a reader. Old man Alexander on helicon tuba. He was in a timing school in the old country. Today, they got him down to Kilbilly as one of the first jazz men. They got a picture of him in a great big thing down in Kilbilly as the first jazz. And this man played no jazz. But he did play with Jacqueline on his funerals. And did he play by ear at all? Oh yeah, he could fake. Any good reader could fake just some bass parts, common chords. Look, if you were a musician, what does it take to fake a common chord? All the chords in the common tunes are almost all identical. They had no accidentals in them. And if you knew one tune, it had to change after so many bars. The chord change would go from, say for instance, you were in, say take the key of B flat. Then you'd go to F7. From F7, you'd go back to B flat. Then B flat 7. Then the top chord, E flat. Then you'd come back to the major chord. Who the devil couldn't play that? You wouldn't have to be a note reader to play that. Faker could play it. Note reader could play it along with a fake band. All they had to do was play. And those men played by music, and they could not play anything jazz. They played ragtime. Like they were playing off their music, and it was a different rhythm. Ragtime had a jumping rhythm. And jazz was a smooth rhythm. It may be a cousin to it, but it has no part of it. In other words, when you play jazz, you're smoothed. You can write ragtime, but you couldn't write jazz. When we had our pieces to be taken down in notation, Miss Claim couldn't put them down. And the men in New York couldn't put them down the way they were. But today, they have signs to put over them. And the men, they know what they are. Why did they know what they are? Because they heard them on the record made by someone before them. I see a realist being around me.
